body.heading: Short and shared beats long and solo
paragraphs: Ten or fifteen minutes of reading together, every night, does more than an occasional long session. The child chooses the book more often than the adult does — rereading a favourite for the twentieth time is not a failure of variety; it is how young readers savour a story.
Take turns with the pages when they are ready: a line each, a character each, or the child reads the speech bubbles. The point is that the book is something you are inside together.

body.heading: The last calm thing
paragraphs: Reading sits well at the end of the day because it slows everything down: voice, breathing, thoughts. A chapter, a poem, or one picture book, then lights lower. Predictability is the sedative — same chair, same blanket, same order of events.
If a child is wired rather than sleepy, choose a calmer book rather than a longer one, and finish at the agreed page even mid-adventure. Stopping at a cliffhanger is also tomorrow's invitation.

body.heading: Let it grow with them
paragraphs: Older children still enjoy being read to long after they can read alone, and listening together to an audiobook on a car journey or while drawing is the same ritual in a new shape. The form can change; the shared story is the tradition.
Keep a note of the books you have read together, even just titles on a kitchen list. It becomes, without trying, a record of their childhood in chapters.

description: A short shared chapter at the end of the day is a reading habit, a calming ritual, and time together in one.
